summary.text: Solar irradiance is the power the Sun delivers as electromagnetic radiation onto each unit of area, measured in watts per square metre.
Above the atmosphere it depends on distance from the Sun and the solar cycle, while at the ground it also depends on surface tilt, the Sun's height and the air.
Measuring it helps predict output from solar power plants, the heating and cooling needs of buildings, and weather and climate.

facts.label: Top of atmosphere
facts.value: About 1361 W/m² on average each year

items.prompt: Sunlight hits the top of the atmosphere at about 1361 W/m² on the side facing the Sun. Averaged over the whole globe, day and night, the figure is about 340 W/m². Why is it divided by four?

options.label: The atmosphere absorbs three quarters of incoming light
A sphere's surface is four times the disc it shows
Earth spends three quarters of each year farther away
Clouds reflect most sunlight back out to space

items.explain: Earth catches sunlight on a disc of area πr² but spreads it over a sphere of area 4πr², so the average is a quarter.

items.prompt: Two identical solar panels sit side by side on a clear day. One lies flat on the ground; the other is angled to face the Sun. Why do they read different irradiance?

options.label: The flat panel is closer to the Earth's warm soil
The angled panel receives light from a different solar cycle
Ground irradiance depends on how the surface is tilted
The flat panel only measures the longest wavelengths

items.explain: At the Earth's surface, irradiance depends on the tilt of the measuring surface as well as the Sun's height and the air.

items.prompt: A satellite far above the air measures sunlight. Which of these can change its reading?

options.label: Cloud cover over the ocean below it
Its distance from the Sun
The humidity of the lower atmosphere
How high the Sun sits above a city's horizon

items.explain: In space, irradiance depends on distance from the Sun and on the solar cycle; clouds and the Sun's height above the horizon only matter at the surface.

items.prompt: Imagine Earth had no atmosphere at all. What would happen to diffuse horizontal irradiance, the light reaching the ground after being scattered across the sky?

options.label: It would become almost zero
It would roughly double
It would match direct sunlight
It would stay about the same

items.explain: Diffuse light comes from the atmosphere scattering sunlight, so without an atmosphere there would be almost none.

items.prompt: An engineer wants the Sun's beam alone, coming straight from the Sun's disc and not scattered light from the rest of the sky. Which measurement fits?

options.label: Diffuse horizontal irradiance
Global tilted irradiance
Direct normal irradiance
Total yearly insolation

items.explain: Direct normal irradiance is measured perpendicular to the Sun's direction and leaves out scattered or reflected sky light.

items.prompt: A homeowner wants to know how much solar energy fell on their roof over a whole month, not how strong the sunlight was at noon. What should they look for?

options.label: The roof's peak irradiance in W/m²
The local solar constant value
The diffuse light's share of the sky
Insolation, irradiance added up over time

items.explain: Adding up irradiance over a period gives the energy received per area, called insolation or solar irradiation, in units like J/m² or kWh/m².
